item.title: The Kiss
item.medium: Oil and gold leaf on canvas
item.lesson: Turn-of-the-century Vienna — the city of Freud, Mahler, and imperial twilight — produced no image more famous than this. Klimt, leader of the Secession movement that broke from the conservative academy, was the son of a gold engraver, and in his 'Golden Phase' he fused that inheritance with the shimmering Byzantine mosaics he had seen at Ravenna: real gold leaf laid over canvas until painting became icon. A couple kneels at the edge of a flowered cliff, wrapped in a single golden mantle that dissolves their bodies into ornament — his marked with hard black-and-white rectangles, hers with soft circles and blooms, masculine and feminine as pure pattern. Only faces, hands, and feet remain flesh. Painted amid whispered scandal around his earlier, more erotic work, The Kiss was an instant, uncomplicated triumph: the Austrian state bought it before it was even finished. Ecstasy, ornament, and a faint vertigo — the lovers kneel at a precipice — in one gilded square.
item.lookFor: Look at her feet: toes curled hard against the cliff edge, tendons taut — the single most human detail in the picture, grounding all that gold in a body's real tension.
